proposal: Week 1: 10 volunteers each propose one project, group votes on top three. Allocate 200 euros per project, pair two volunteers per project. Week 2-3: twice-weekly 30-min check-ins. Week 4: final inspection. Stalled project: remaining volunteers meet, vote to reassign 200 euros to next backup project within 48 hours.

proposal: Organize a two-hour "Story Table Exchange" inside the empty room. Each of six volunteers brings one household item (under 5 €) that reminds them of their town. Participants sit in a circle, place items on a shared cloth, and in three rounds of seven minutes each, explain the memory and listen without interruption. After every round they rotate seats. At the end, a volunteer photographs the table and prints six postcard-size copies for participants to keep and later swap. Budget: 30 € for printing and refreshments; the remaining 270 € stays untouched. No special equipment or expert skills are required, and the event can be scheduled within two weeks.

proposal: Day 1: call for project ideas from residents. Day 3: vote selects three projects. Day 5: each pair receives 200 euros and a written task list. Days 7, 14, 21, 28: 15-minute check-ins. If stalled, pair reports; funds and volunteers shift to active projects within 48 hours. Final inspection on day 30.

proposal: Divide twelve adults into six pairs. Each pair receives one sub-skill written on an index card. Meeting 1: 45 minutes hands-on practice with stationery props, 15 minutes peer teaching. Meeting 2: pairs rotate, chain all sub-skills, perform live demonstration. Success: complete demonstration without cards.

task.prompt: A public library wants to help twelve adults learn a difficult practical skill together. They have two one-hour meetings, ordinary stationery, and no paid teacher or internet connection. Design one original learning method, explain why it could work, and make its success observable. Maximum 180 words.

proposal: Participants form four stations: inspection, disassembly, repair, documentation. Each person draws a role card for a 25-minute shift. Broken objects rotate clockwise. A 'parts-only' bin holds pieces that cannot be fixed, preventing over-promise. Success measured by number of objects leaving with a written status tag (fixed, spare-parts, or recycle) and a brief photo log. Safeguard: a visible timer and a 'next station' bell limits any single person's time with an object.

task.prompt: A neighborhood group has twenty broken everyday objects, one table, basic hand tools, and participants with mixed levels of confidence. Design one original process that reduces waste and encourages participation without promising that every object can be repaired. Include a practical safeguard and a way to assess success. Maximum 180 words.

proposal: Each resident receives five colored dots as tokens. Individuals place dots beside posted activity proposals to express interest strength. Highest-scoring activities receive priority slots. Remaining dots fund second choices. A scribe transfers the ranked list onto a calendar grid. The group initials each block. The completed calendar is taped to the noticeboard before leaving.

task.prompt: Eight residents have one hour to plan the use of a shared courtyard for the next month. They have paper, pens and a noticeboard. Propose a meeting format and a way to put its result into practice. Maximum 180 words.

proposal: Process: 1) Morning circle lists each object’s owner, function, and visible damage. 2) Three stations: quick-fix (5–15 min with pliers/screwdrivers), deep-fix (30–60 min with extra hands), and creative-upcycle (repurpose parts). 3) Participants choose station by confidence; experts rotate to coach. 4) Unrepairable pieces go to labeled donation bin for parts harvest or local recycler. Practical safeguard: color-coded time-limit cards (green 15 min, yellow 45 min) prevent monopolizing tools. Success metric: track objects leaving in one of three states—fixed, repurposed, or responsibly diverted—target 60 % diversion from landfill within one session.

proposal: Round 1: Form six pairs. Each pair receives one numbered step of the skill on an index card. Pair A teaches its step to Pair B while both watch and note one observable success marker (e.g., 'thread passes smoothly'). After five minutes, Pair B teaches the same step back. Round 2: Pairs rotate clockwise and repeat with the next step. Each pair ends with a checklist of twelve verified markers. Success is observable when every checklist is fully ticked within the two hours.

proposal: Round-robin proposal: each resident lists one idea for 2 min. Quick show-of-hands ranking narrows to three options. Eight residents then sign a calendar grid showing day, time, and task. Grid taped to noticeboard within five minutes.

proposal: Method: 12 learners pair up and teach each other one practical step per round using only pen-and-paper diagrams. Each pair creates a 5-minute demo, then swaps partners. After four rounds, pairs present the full skill in a 5-minute show-and-tell. Success is observable when every pair demonstrates the complete skill error-free within the allotted time.

proposal: Six volunteers set two tables in the empty room, label one Swap and one Story. Budget buys tea, biscuits and index cards. Each resident arrives with one item, places it on Swap and speaks for two minutes about its story. Listeners may trade. After 90 minutes, volunteers collect contact cards so participants can continue meeting. Sessions run every Wednesday and Saturday for four weeks.

proposal: Coordinator lists ten discrete jobs and assigns each privately. Volunteers sign pledge with date and cost limit. Materials bought only after pledge and receipt scan. Any delay over three days moves task to next volunteer; original volunteer loses their €60 slice.

proposal: Residents will receive pre-cut paper sheets and shared stencils. On four Saturdays they add one line, word or colour to a growing communal mural. A volunteer curator staples each contribution daily. At week’s end a brief anonymous survey asks what the mural means to participants; results are posted beside the finished work.

task.prompt: A library has a blank wall, donated paper and four Saturday afternoons. Design a public exhibition that residents can contribute to without artistic training. Explain how it will be assembled, maintained and evaluated. Maximum 180 words.

proposal: With 90 euros, volunteers buy 30 cotton squares, permanent markers, needles and thread. The remaining 210 euros covers two portable sewing machines rented for one day. Flyers invite residents to bring one photo or object that sparks a memory. On the day, pairs spend 30 minutes interviewing and drawing. Squares are pinned to a frame; volunteers help stitch them into a 1.5 m × 2 m banner. The finished quilt is hung in the town hall for one month, with names and meeting dates written on a tag so participants can reconnect later.

proposal: Use a timed agenda: 5 min intro, 20 min round-robin ideas on the board, 20 min ranking by dot-voting, 10 min assign roles, 5 min confirm dates. Post the signed schedule on the noticeboard and each resident initials their slot before leaving.

Maintain: daily tape check 9am; replace loose slips immediately. Evaluate: count slips weekly, tally comment-card ratings 1-5, report to library board.

In session one they write step-by-step instructions on paper, then rotate tables to test and annotate every other group’s instructions. Session two they merge the best instructions into a single manual and practice the full skill in pairs. Success is visible when every participant can perform the complete skill using only the final manual.

proposal: Rotating peer-teach: each of 12 adults receives one unique 5-minute segment of the skill (via printed cue cards). During hour 1, every person teaches their segment to two rotating partners; hour 2 is full-group practice with silent observers noting one observable checklist item per learner. Success is measured when each checklist records ≥10 correct demonstrations by session end.

proposal: Divide into two groups of four. Each group uses ten minutes to list three courtyard rules on separate cards. Cards are swapped, and each group ranks the other's rules. Top six rules become the operating code. A drawn timetable grid is pinned; residents sign up for preferred half-days in marker. The grid is photographed on a phone and the photo printed and re-pinned weekly for updates.
